# Session 2: LSTM Drought Monitoring Lab

### Hands-on LSTM Forecasting of Sentinel-2 NDVI for Mindanao

Forecast next month's vegetation condition for Bukidnon and South Cotabato and turn the forecast into drought alerts
:::

## Session Overview

This 2.5-hour lab puts the LSTM theory from Session 1 into practice on real data. You load a monthly Sentinel-2 NDVI series for two Mindanao provinces (live from Google Earth Engine, or from a cached sample), build sliding-window training samples, train a two-layer LSTM in **PyTorch**, check it against simple baselines and turn its forecasts into drought alerts.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

1. **Retrieve** a monthly, cloud-masked Sentinel-2 NDVI time series for a province with Google Earth Engine
2. **Create** supervised training samples with a sliding window (12 months in → 1 month out)
3. **Split and scale** time series data without leakage (temporal train/validation/test split, scaler fitted on training data only)
4. **Build and train** an LSTM in PyTorch with early stopping
5. **Evaluate** forecasts with MAE and RMSE against persistence and seasonal baselines
6. **Translate** forecasts into drought alerts and score them with precision and recall
:::

## Case Study: Mindanao Drought Monitoring

### Why Bukidnon and South Cotabato?

**Bukidnon** (about 10,500 km², largely an upland plateau) and **South Cotabato** (about 3,900 km²) are major agricultural provinces in Mindanao: corn, rice, pineapple, coffee, sugarcane and vegetables. Much of the farmland is rain-fed, so it is sensitive to rainfall deficits.

**Climate challenges:**

- El Niño episodes bring below-normal rainfall, dry spells and drought to Mindanao; the 2015-2016, 2019 and 2023-2024 events all caused crop losses
- Mindanao's rainfall regime differs between provinces (PAGASA climate types III and IV), so "dry season" timing is local
- Inter-annual variability makes fixed calendars unreliable

::: {.callout-important}
## Why forecasting matters

Agencies such as the Department of Agriculture (DA) and PAGASA need **lead time** to act on drought: adjusting planting calendars, scheduling irrigation, positioning seed and crop insurance support, and issuing farm advisories. A forecast of next month's vegetation condition is one input to that decision; it does not replace PAGASA's climate outlooks or field reports.
:::

### Study area and data

| Item | Lab setting |
|---|---|
| Areas | Rough bounding boxes around Bukidnon and South Cotabato (use official boundaries for real work) |
| Sensor | Sentinel-2 surface reflectance, `COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED` in Earth Engine |
| Cloud masking | Scene Classification Layer (SCL): keep vegetation, bare soil and water pixels |
| Land mask | ESA WorldCover 2021 cropland (class 40) |
| Aggregation | Monthly median composite → province mean NDVI |
| Period | Cached sample: 2018-2023; live fetch default: 2019-2025 |

## Lab Workflow

The student and instructor notebooks have the same 16 parts.

### Parts 1-5: Setup and data (30 minutes)

Imports, random seeds and device; an optional Earth Engine connection; study areas; the NDVI helper; data loading. Earth Engine is **off by default**, so the lab always works with the cached sample. To use live data:

```python
USE_EARTH_ENGINE = True
EE_PROJECT = "your-cloud-project"     # a Cloud project registered for Earth Engine

import ee
ee.Authenticate()                     # once per user / runtime
ee.Initialize(project=EE_PROJECT)
```

The helper `fetch_monthly_ndvi()` builds the monthly, cloud-masked, cropland-only NDVI series with one Earth Engine request per province and year. In the student notebook it is an optional stretch exercise; if it is not implemented or the request fails, the notebook falls back to the cached sample.

### Parts 6-7: Exploration (20 minutes)

Plot both provinces against an illustrative NDVI = 0.40 threshold and compute seasonal means and the lowest month per province. Discuss: which years dip lowest, and do the two provinces behave the same way?

### Parts 8-10: Sequences, split and scaling (30 minutes)

```python
LOOKBACK, HORIZON = 12, 1   # 12 months in, next month out
for idx in range(LOOKBACK, len(values) - HORIZON + 1):
    history = values[idx - LOOKBACK:idx]
    target = values[idx + HORIZON - 1]
```

- **Temporal split:** the last year is the test set, the year before is validation, everything earlier is training (cached sample: 72 / 24 / 24 samples)
- **No leakage:** min-max scaling uses the training months only

::: {.callout-warning}
## Avoid data leakage

Never shuffle a time series *before* splitting it, and never fit a scaler on the whole series. Both let the model "see" the test period and make results look better than they will be in operation.
:::

### Parts 11-13: PyTorch model and training (40 minutes)

```python
class NDVIForecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=1, hidden_sizes=(64, 32), dropout=0.2):
        super().__init__()
        self.lstm1 = nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_sizes[0], batch_first=True)
        self.lstm2 = nn.LSTM(hidden_sizes[0], hidden_sizes[1], batch_first=True)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(hidden_sizes[1], 16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16, 1))

    def forward(self, x):
        out, _ = self.lstm1(x)
        out, _ = self.lstm2(self.dropout(out))
        return self.head(self.dropout(out[:, -1, :]))   # last time step
```

Training uses Adam (learning rate 0.001), MSE loss, up to 150 epochs and early stopping on validation loss (patience 20), keeping the best weights.

### Parts 14-16: Evaluation and alerts (30 minutes)

- Learning curves (train vs validation MSE and MAE)
- Test-year MAE and RMSE in NDVI units, compared with two baselines:
  - **persistence:** next month = this month
  - **seasonal naive:** next month = the same month last year
- Drought alerts: NDVI < 0.40, confusion table, precision and recall

::: {.callout-tip}
## Read the baseline comparison carefully

With only six years of monthly data (72 training samples on the cached sample), persistence is a strong baseline and the LSTM may only match it. That is a useful result: it shows how much data an LSTM needs and motivates pooling more locations, adding covariates, or using pre-trained features (Session 3).
:::

## Exercises

1. **Exploration (Part 6):** which months are lowest in each province? Do the 2019 values look different from other years?
2. **Training (Part 13):** at which epoch did early stopping trigger? Do the learning curves show overfitting?
3. **Evaluation (Part 15):** does the LSTM beat persistence? Where are the largest errors?
4. **Alerts (Part 16):** how many drought months does the test year contain? What does that mean for precision and recall?
5. **Stretch:** set `HORIZON = 3` and compare errors; or implement `fetch_monthly_ndvi()` and rerun with live data.

## Operational Deployment Considerations

### From notebook to service

1. **Data acquisition:** Sentinel-2 NDVI from Earth Engine or the [CopPhil Infrastructure](https://infra.copphil.philsa.gov.ph) (Copernicus mirror site hosted at PhilSA); rainfall and temperature from PAGASA; the ENSO index ([ONI](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/ensostuff/ONI_v5.php)) from NOAA
2. **Preprocessing:** cloud masking, monthly compositing, aggregation to municipality or province, cropland masking
3. **Inference:** monthly forecasts for 1 and (with caution) 3 months ahead, ideally with uncertainty (ensembles or Monte Carlo dropout)
4. **Alerting:** thresholds agreed with users, preferably on anomalies relative to each area's normal rather than a fixed NDVI value
5. **Communication:** dashboards and advisories for DA, PAGASA and LGUs

```python
# Pseudo-code for a monthly forecasting job (functions are placeholders)
def monthly_drought_forecast():
    ndvi = fetch_latest_ndvi(region="Bukidnon", months=12)   # Earth Engine / CopPhil
    X = scale(ndvi)[None, :, None]                            # (1, 12, 1)
    forecast = invert(model(torch.tensor(X)).item())
    if forecast < DROUGHT_THRESHOLD:
        notify(["DA", "PAGASA", "LGUs"], f"Predicted NDVI {forecast:.2f} next month")
    return forecast
```

### Model maintenance

- Retrain at least yearly as new data arrives; monitor error against what actually happened
- Version models, training data and thresholds; keep a rollback option
- Collect qualitative feedback (did farmers and LGUs observe drought when the model said so?)

---

## Troubleshooting Guide

**Overfitting (training loss ≪ validation loss):** increase dropout (0.3-0.4), reduce units (32/16), add weight decay to Adam, add more locations or years.

**Loss not decreasing:** lower the learning rate (1e-4), check that scaling uses [0, 1], simplify the model.

**Predictions lag one month behind the actual values:** the model has learned persistence. Add covariates (rainfall, ONI, soil moisture), predict anomalies instead of raw NDVI, or use a longer lookback.

**Large errors at drought onset:** droughts are rare in a short record. Weight drought months more in the loss, add ENSO information, or combine with other models.

**Earth Engine errors:** check that your Cloud project is registered for Earth Engine and passed to `ee.Initialize(project=...)`; reduce the period or increase `scale` if a request times out. The cached sample always works.

---

## Extensions

- **Multivariate inputs:** rainfall, temperature, ONI, Sentinel-1 backscatter (`input_size > 1`)
- **Multi-step forecasting:** `HORIZON = 3`, or sequence-to-sequence output
- **Many locations:** municipalities or pixels instead of two province means; ConvLSTM for spatial fields
- **Uncertainty:** Monte Carlo dropout or small ensembles
- **Explainability:** Integrated Gradients with [Captum](https://captum.ai/) to see which past months drive a forecast (Session 3)

---

## Key Takeaways

::: {.callout-important}
## Session 2 Summary

- A monthly, cloud-masked, cropland-only NDVI series is a practical starting point for drought forecasting
- Sliding windows turn a time series into supervised samples; the split must be temporal and scaling must use training data only
- The LSTM design from Session 1 carries over directly from Keras to PyTorch
- Always compare against simple baselines; with short records they are hard to beat
- Alerts need agreed thresholds and evaluation with precision and recall, and rare events make that evaluation uncertain
:::
